items.title: Researcher runs 600 experiments on JEPA world models, finds hierarchical planning and latent memory graphs significantly improve long-horizon task success [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
items.summary:
A researcher conducted 600 experiments on the JEPA (joint-embedding predictive architecture) world model LeWM, which is designed for long-horizon robotic tasks like pushing a block to a target position. The study found that LeWM's predictions are as effective as perfect physics for planning over 25-step horizons, but performance drops over longer horizons without additional strategies.

The researcher identified four new planning methods that improved LeWM's success rate on 75-step tasks from 22% to 85% without retraining. Key improvements included hierarchical planning by chaining 25-step subgoals and using a latent memory graph constructed from expert demonstrations to select reachable subgoals. These methods outperformed simply swapping in perfect physics, highlighting the importance of planning architecture over prediction accuracy in JEPA models.

items.title: Clowder launches a Mac status board for managing multiple Claude AI coding sessions with color-coded tiles indicating session states [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sick of Herding AI Cats?
items.summary:
Clowder is a native macOS app designed to help users monitor multiple Claude AI coding sessions simultaneously by displaying each session as a colored tile indicating its status, such as needing user input, ready, working, or idle. The app supports up to four tiles for free and runs on macOS 14 or later with Apple silicon.

The app tracks five different Claude session types on the user's Mac without requiring sign-in or sending data externally. It uses color, brightness, movement, and tile age to signal urgency and session state, helping users quickly identify which sessions require attention. Clowder aims to simplify the bookkeeping involved in managing multiple AI sessions across various work environments.

items.title: DeepSeek releases V4 Pro 0813 open weights model with 1M token context window, below-average intelligence, higher cost, and slower performance compared to similar models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813
items.summary:
DeepSeek has released the V4 Pro 0813 model, an open weights AI model supporting text input and output with a 1 million token context window. The model scores 23 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, placing it below average among comparable open weights models of similar size, and it is slower and more expensive per task than the median for its class. Pricing is $1.32 per million input tokens and $3.96 per million output tokens, with an average evaluation time of 19.9 minutes per task, compared to a median of 14 minutes.

The model's verbosity is somewhat higher than average, generating 119 million tokens during evaluation versus a median of 104 million. DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 is categorized among 131 similar models and is assessed using multiple benchmarks including reasoning, knowledge work, and coding tasks. The release includes detailed performance, cost, and intelligence metrics to help users compare it with other open weights AI models.

items.title: Researchers develop Zugwise to digitize handwritten chess scoresheets by reconstructing entire games and detecting implausible moves using computer chess techniques [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Zugwise: Domain-Aware Game Reconstruction for Digitizing Handwritten Chess Scoresheets
items.summary:
Researchers have created Zugwise, a system that digitizes handwritten chess scoresheets by reconstructing full games rather than just recognizing individual moves. It uses computer chess methods to identify moves that a human player is unlikely to have written, making subtle errors more detectable than traditional legality checks. The system combines data from both players' scoresheets and employs backward search to trace errors, significantly reducing silent mistakes in digitization.

Zugwise operates entirely in the browser, ensuring privacy and offline capability, and introduces a three-way adjudication protocol for verifying records when no single source is definitive. In tests on tournament data, it reduced silent errors substantially and improved the accuracy of move corrections using learned signals without requiring retraining on new data.

items.title: Researchers find that editing an AI agent's error history can reduce performance if the real-world state still contains those errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Cleaning an Agent's History Hurts When the World Still Holds the Error
items.summary:
A study investigates how modifying the recorded history of mistakes made by tool-using language-model agents affects their task success when the actual environment still holds those errors. The research shows that simply correcting the history without updating the world state can worsen outcomes, as demonstrated by experiments where truthful notes improved recovery but presenting completed actions without corresponding world changes decreased performance.

The experiments involved freezing an agent mid-task and altering either its history or the world state, revealing that the effectiveness of history edits depends on their consistency with the real-world state. For example, reporting success for an action that failed in the world lowered task success, while accurate reporting aligned with the world improved it. These findings highlight the importance of synchronizing history corrections with the actual state to avoid degrading agent performance.

The research shows that simply correcting the history without addressing the underlying world state can sometimes worsen outcomes. These findings highlight that the effectiveness of history edits depends on their consistency with the world's actual state, and that making a history appear clean while errors persist in the world can be detrimental.

items.summary: Together AI has developed the Together Compiler (TKCC), a continual compilation system designed to optimize AI inference workloads that frequently change in model architecture and traffic patterns. TKCC introduces a Tiered Persistent Engine to reduce engine launch overhead and a cost model to select parallelism configurations, addressing the tradeoff between measurement throughput and fidelity. The system outperforms existing hand-optimized kernels and open-source engines on various language models, achieving state-of-the-art throughput per second (TPS) including at batch size one. TKCC is deployed in production, processing trillions of tokens across Together AI's infrastructure, and generalizes beyond language model inference.

items.title: Study examines integration of semantic priors from large language models into partially-identified causal discovery, highlighting challenges in query allocation, proposal admission, and graph retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Should Semantic Priors Enter Partially-Identified Causal Discovery?
items.summary:
A recent study investigates how semantic information from large language models can aid observational causal discovery, which often leaves causal directions unresolved or unstable. The research focuses on decisions about where to apply semantic queries, which semantic proposals to accept, and which causal graphs to retain, aiming to improve causal inference accuracy.

Experiments on benchmark networks show that semantic information improves causal recovery compared to random orientations, but targeting unstable edges offers no clear advantage over random allocation. The study also finds that current methods for admitting semantic proposals lack effective calibration, and the adequacy of reference data significantly affects the retention of causal graphs. These results identify calibration size and reference adequacy as key limitations in effectively incorporating semantic priors into causal discovery processes.

items.originalTitle: SynthCorp: A Platform for Creating Benchmarks for Data Agents
items.summary: SynthCorp is a platform designed to generate customizable data environments and benchmarks by simulating business events that produce and modify corporate data over time. It integrates relational databases, document stores, and data catalogs, scheduling events on a virtual calendar to build consistent data estates and generate analytical tasks with verified solutions. The platform has produced initial benchmarks featuring multiple data estates and tasks across various domains, enabling evaluation of model performance and data contexts without manual annotation. SynthCorp aims to support the development of advanced enterprise data agents by providing complex, targeted benchmarking scenarios that expose reasoning challenges in current models.

items.title: Study finds humans use Bayesian inference on timing cues for social coordination in The Mind game, while AI models struggle to adapt behaviorally over time [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Rational Use of Time for Social Coordination in Humans and AI
items.summary:
A study examined how humans and AI use temporal cues for social coordination in the cooperative card game The Mind, which prohibits explicit communication and relies solely on timing signals. Researchers tested 150 human participants alongside two AI model types—computer-use agents and text-prompted large language models—and found humans employ a Bayesian strategy to infer partners' beliefs from timing, a method partially mirrored by advanced AI models. However, unlike humans, the AI models did not effectively adapt their behavior to their partners during repeated interactions.

The findings suggest humans engage in implicit probabilistic reasoning about continuous-time signals in dynamic social settings, a capability that may arise without direct real-time experience. The study highlights challenges for AI systems in interpreting and adapting to implicit temporal signals for efficient coordination with other agents in dynamic environments.

items.title: Researchers find preference-based language model leaderboards using Bradley-Terry model vulnerable to manipulation via strategic voting, prompting, and nomination, boosting ranks by up to 45 places [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Leaderboard Hacking: Preference-Based Model Evaluations are Vulnerable to Manipulation
items.summary: A study reveals that arena-style rankings of language models, which rely on pairwise comparisons and the Bradley-Terry model, are susceptible to manipulation strategies including strategic voting, prompting, and nomination. These tactics can artificially inflate a model's rank by up to 45 places when combined, as demonstrated on public leaderboard data. The vulnerabilities affect any preference-based evaluation framework that allows open prompting, voting, or model submission using the Bradley-Terry model. The researchers also propose safeguards to mitigate these manipulation risks.

items.title: Researchers propose Minimal Belief Set method for robust state estimation using pretrained Vision-Language Models, improving decision-making and computational efficiency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Robust Task-Aware State Estimation from Pre-trained Perception
items.summary: Researchers have developed a method to improve state estimation in agents using pretrained perception models like Vision-Language Models (VLMs) by constructing a minimal set of likely states called the \(\theta\)-confidence Minimal Belief Set (MBS\(_\theta\)). This approach balances robustness and computational efficiency by focusing on the most probable states rather than relying on a single best-guess or a full probability distribution. The method uses a three-layered belief system and an algorithm named Probability-Ranked Valid State Search (PRaVaSS) to efficiently generate the MBS\(_\theta\) with theoretical guarantees. Validation with a VLM backbone shows scalability and improved downstream decision-making in task-planning scenarios.

items.title: Study evaluates proof-step verification using LLM judges for open-weight mathematical reasoning, finding precision gains but limited coverage and distinct failure modes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Is Proof-Step Verification Worth Its Cost? Operating Requirements of Certify-or-Decline Verification for Open-Weight Mathematical Reasoning
items.summary:
Researchers assess a proof-step verification pipeline that rewrites solver answers into typed steps and uses large language model (LLM) judges to certify or decline them across datasets including GPQA, AIME-2025, and MATH-500. Certification improves answer-key-match precision significantly on GPQA and AIME but covers only a fraction of attempts, while gains on near-ceiling MATH-500 are minimal and come with reduced coverage. A self-consistency selector achieves comparable precision at similar coverage levels, and diagnostic analysis reveals many problems fail due to invalid proof construction before reaching judgment.

External LLM acceptance rates of certified proofs are lower than answer-key matches, and audits lack human or formal ground truth, with near-zero agreement between open-weight auditor pairs indicating consistency issues rather than accuracy. The findings suggest the need for separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity, with detailed per-configuration results provided in the supplement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof-step verification rewrites a solver's answer into typed steps and uses LLM judges to certify or decline. We evaluate this pipeline on open-weight models across GPQA, AIME-2025, and a MATH-500 subset. Certification raises answer-key-match precision by 31 percentage points on the strong GPQA configuration and 46 on AIME, while answering only 35% and 21% of attempts. On near-ceiling MATH-500, gains are at most 5 points at a loss of 13-27 points of coverage. An output-token-matched self-consistency selector obtains 82.9% precision at 35% coverage, compared with the verifier's pooled 87.6% (paired difference: +4.8 points, 95% interval [-8.2, 18.5]). A diagnostic sample reveals a distinct failure mode: 52 of 88 completed problems end in invalid proof construction without ever reaching a judge. Finally, external-LLM acceptance of rendered certified chains is 61.0-67.6%, compared with 87.6% answer-key match. These audits lack human or formal-kernel ground truth. Open-weight auditor pairs show near-zero chance-corrected agreement, which measures consistency rather than accuracy against proof truth. These results motivate separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity. We provide per-configuration results and evaluation details in the supplement.

The findings suggest the need for separate reporting of execution failures, selected-answer precision, and independently assessed proof validity, with detailed per-configuration results provided in the supplement.

items.title: Researchers propose GenPFN, a training-free tabular foundation model to augment small engineering datasets by generating and refining candidate designs using a pretrained TabPFN classifier [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: GenPFN: An In-Context Tabular Foundation Model Approach for Augmenting Small Datasets in Engineering
items.summary:
GenPFN is a candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier that interpolates between desired engineering designs and refines them using classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. The method evaluates candidates against problem constraints and objectives, augmenting limited datasets to improve regression model training.

The approach was tested on fourteen engineering problems, including a 44-parameter hull design, and outperformed adversarial, variational-autoencoder, and diffusion generators in class satisfaction and realism distance. Compared to SMOTE, GenPFN achieved lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Augmentation with GenPFN reduced AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to training on context data alone. A hull-stern case study showed 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% from random sampling, demonstrating GenPFN's potential to enhance predictive modeling with small datasets.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14804v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Costly simulations and experiments limit the data available for engineering design. This paper proposes GenPFN, a training-free candidate generator guided by a pretrained tabular Prior-Data Fitted Network (TabPFN) classifier with fixed weights. The context contains evaluated designs labeled desired (Class 1) or undesired (Class 0). GenPFN interpolates between desired designs and refines candidates using gated classifier gradients and Gaussian noise. Each candidate is evaluated using the problem's constraints and objective functions. Evaluated desired designs and their objective values augment the context for regression training. Evaluation spans fourteen selected problems, including a two-parameter benchmark and a 44-parameter hull problem. In paired comparisons, GenPFN with TabPFN v1 achieves higher class satisfaction and lower realism distance than the tested adversarial, variational-autoencoder and diffusion generators. The variational-autoencoder generator provides greater coverage and diversity. Relative to the synthetic minority over-sampling technique (SMOTE), GenPFN provides lower coverage distance and greater diversity. Among observed paired regression fits, augmentation reduces estimated AutoGluon validation mean squared error by 62.1% relative to context-only training. A hull-stern case study yields 99.3% propeller-compatible candidates versus 1.4% among randomly sampled context designs. Generation followed by evaluation produces sample sets that augment limited datasets and support training more accurate predictive models.

items.title: Researchers develop AutoAssumption, a system that searches over algorithmic assumptions to discover and improve ML system algorithms, formalizing 89 methods with explicit proofs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AutoAssumption: Searching over Assumptions Discovers ML-Systems Algorithms
items.summary:
Researchers introduced AutoAssumption, a framework that formalizes machine learning system algorithms as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, enabling a search over these assumptions to discover and improve algorithms. The system was applied to 89 algorithms in KV-cache eviction, weight pruning, and speculative decoding, producing state-of-the-art results and generating verified code.

AutoAssumption relaxes assumptions of existing methods, re-derives and re-proves them, and outperforms published algorithms in key tasks, achieving the highest RULER-4K score for eviction and lowest perplexity for pruning on multiple LLaMA models. The approach leverages large language models and proof checkers to explore a structured space of algorithm designs, with future work aiming to formalize more fields and integrate shared assumptions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many advances in ML systems came from breaking an assumption that earlier methods took for granted: speculative decoding dropped the assumption that a model needs one forward pass per token. Yet algorithms rarely state their assumptions, so experts and discovery harnesses search over programs, where one edit changes several design choices and gains are difficult to attribute. Searching over the assumptions themselves remains largely unexplored. Writing algorithms as proofs makes their assumptions explicit and turns algorithm design into a search over a small, structured space that an LLM can explore and a proof checker can audit. We formalize 89 algorithms from KV-cache eviction, weight pruning and speculative decoding as proof graphs with explicit assumptions, checked in Lean. Our harness, AutoAssumption, relaxes one assumption of a published method, re-derives and re-proves it, and generates its code. In KV-cache eviction and weight pruning, this search improved on every published algorithm we ran and produced state-of-the-art algorithms. The eviction algorithm has the highest RULER-4K score of the published methods we ran, and the pruning algorithm the lowest perplexity of thirteen on four LLaMA models. At equal budget, the harness scores within a point of OpenEvolve, an open-source implementation of AlphaEvolve, with a lower standard deviation across repeats. Future work will formalize more fields and combine them through the principal assumptions they share.

items.title: Researchers outline computational challenges and approaches in human-agent systems for effective interaction and decision-making under uncertainty [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Open Challenges and Opportunities in Human-Agent Systems
items.summary:
This paper examines the challenges and opportunities in human-agent systems where AI agents perform extended tasks on behalf of people, emphasizing the importance of understanding human perspectives and coordinating capabilities. It reviews foundational computational methods from the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems community, including Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, and cooperative learning, to support interactions ranging from individual partnerships to larger groups with diverse roles and objectives.

The authors organize these approaches around the dual challenges of representing and inferring mental states and deciding how to interact, highlighting mechanisms such as observer-aware planning and decision-theoretic communication. They argue that advancing human-agent interaction requires treating it as an ongoing decision problem influenced by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting goals, to better align evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations with agent actions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic AI systems increasingly undertake extended tasks and act on people's behalf, making human-agent interaction central to their effectiveness. Successful interaction requires understanding human perspectives, coordinating complementary capabilities, and maintaining productive relationships within socio-technical environments. This paper examines how foundations developed by the Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (AAMAS) community inform these demands. We consider interactions ranging from individual human-agent partnerships to teams and larger groups, where participants differ in their roles, decision authority, capabilities, and objectives. We organize computational approaches around the connected challenges of understanding others and deciding how to interact with them. Theory of Mind, belief-desire-intention architectures, goal and plan recognition, inverse planning, and recursive reasoning provide mechanisms for representing and inferring partially observable mental states. Observer-aware planning, model reconciliation, and decision-theoretic communication connect these inferences to action, explanation, and information exchange. Together with shared autonomy, argumentation, and cooperative inverse reinforcement learning, these approaches offer foundations for agentic systems that account for evolving human knowledge, intentions, and expectations. We argue that progress requires treating human interaction as an ongoing decision problem shaped by uncertainty, interdependence, and potentially conflicting objectives.

items.title: Researchers propose vocabulary support reduction in language-model distillation to cut training costs without degrading performance on reasoning tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Effective Teacher Support for Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: Researchers introduce a method to reduce the vocabulary fraction used in forward-KL language-model distillation, focusing on the teacher's highest-probability tokens and renormalizing the retained mass from 100% down to 0.01%. This approach was tested on Qwen3 and Nemotron Nano model pairs, showing no significant degradation in MMLU-Pro reasoning task performance even at very low vocabulary support levels. The method reduces training step time by 38% and peak memory usage by 24% without harming evaluation metrics. The study highlights that the optimal vocabulary cutoff depends on the model family, with smaller fractions sometimes failing to produce expected reasoning tags.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.14850v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Forward-KL language-model distillation normally computes dense teacher and student scores over the full vocabulary at every supervised position, making training and stored teacher targets expensive. We instead distill from the teacher's highest-probability vocabulary fraction, renormalizing the retained mass as we sweep support from 100% to 0.01%. Our main study distills Qwen3 4B -> 1.7B. We confirm the broader support-reduction finding on larger Qwen3 8B -> 4B and Nemotron Nano 12B -> 9B pairs and under answer-only supervision. We evaluate generation primarily on MMLU-Pro and secondarily on GPQA-Diamond. Across the Qwen3 settings, retaining 0.01% of the vocabulary causes no observed MMLU-Pro degradation relative to full-vocabulary distillation, although disagreement with the complete teacher distribution increases. Nemotron Nano matches full-vocabulary MMLU-Pro at 0.1%, but smaller fractions fail to emit the closing reasoning tag, showing that the reliable cutoff depends on the model family. At 0.01% support, caching the retained next-token scores from the teacher forward pass cuts training step time by 38%, while restricting student output computation to those tokens cuts peak memory by 24%; neither causes observed MMLU-Pro degradation.

items.title: Can an AI Agent Be Epistemically Akratic? Higher-Order Evidence & the Limits of Self-Correction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can an AI Agent Be Epistemically Akratic? Higher-Order Evidence & the Limits of Self-Correction
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14889v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When we judge that our reasoning was defective, it seems plausible that we should abandon the conclusion it produced. This thought has special force for AI agents built to assess and correct their own work. Yet obeying such judgments can make an agent worse at distinguishing sound reasoning from defective reasoning. An AI agent may rely on information about its reasoning when deciding which conclusions to keep, while the part that judges whether those conclusions are justified cannot use that information. The agent can then exercise an epistemic competence by retaining conclusions it judges unjustified, even when its self-assessments are generally reliable. Nor is the difficulty resolved by training the agent to make its conclusions and assessments agree: agreement can be achieved by degrading either one. Crucially, I argue that a negative assessment can remain valuable by identifying conclusions requiring further scrutiny, without having authority to eliminate them. The result challenges a central assumption about AI self-correction: that bringing an agent's beliefs into agreement with its own self-assessment about their justification makes it better at correcting its mistakes.

items.title: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MuEdit: An efficient multi-task editing method towards inter-domain knowledge conflicts
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14910v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) require frequent knowledge updates across heterogeneous domains, but existing editing methods fail when applied sequentially to multi-task settings. We trace this collapse to inter-domain null-space misalignment: heterogeneous tasks induce distinct Jacobian geometries, causing their common null space to shrink dramatically and leaving insufficient admissible directions for conflict-free updates. We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

We propose the Conflict Index to quantify this geometric interference, and introduce Mu-Edit, which mitigates multi-task conflicts via (1) conflict-aware ordering to minimize cumulative interference, and (2) dynamic low-rank approximation to expand the null space when ordering alone is insufficient. Experiments across five functional domains and three backbones show that Mu-Edit significantly outperforms existing baselines in multi-task editing performance while preserving general capabilities, and remains effective under incremental task arrival.

items.title: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Edge-Native Multimodal RAG: Hardware-Aware Quantization and Architectural Optimization for Consumer GPUs
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14924v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deployment of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for Edge-AI is constrained by memory and bandwidth limitations. A standard 7B parameter model consumes 14 GB Video Random Access Memory (VRAM) in half-precision (FP16), precluding co-location of vector indices and Key-Value (KV) caches. This paper presents an engineering integration and empirical evaluation of a multimodal RAG framework optimized for consumer-grade Turing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA Tesla T4). Our system-level analysis identifies a critical trade-off: while generative pre-trained transformer quantization (GPTQ) offers superior throughput (51.6 tok/s), it exhibits significant context instability at 2048+ tokens on Turing architectures. Conversely, NormalFloat 4-bit (NF4) maintains robust long-context performance with viable latency (81 ms/tok). By coupling NF4 with a decoupled Florence-2 vision integration, we achieve visual reasoning with only 430 MB VRAM overhead. Furthermore, empirical observations of prompt-induced search space pruning show that structured prompting reduces latency by 47% without altering computational intensity (1.88 GFLOPs/token). The integrated architecture maintains an 8.37 GB footprint, establishing a viable RAG pipeline for 12-16 GB GPUs. Finally, structured few-shot prompting effectively compensates for quantization-induced reasoning loss, restoring mathematical accuracy from 35.0% to 92.0% across 200 trials.

items.title: Provably Optimal HBT Legalization in Seconds: Certified Optima Reveal Where the Headroom Really Lies [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Provably Optimal HBT Legalization in Seconds: Certified Optima Reveal Where the Headroom Really Lies
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid bonding terminal (HBT) legalization assigns every terminal of a face-to-face 3D IC to its own pitch-grid site with minimum total Manhattan displacement. Open3DBench reports that a reinforcement-learning (RL) legalizer reduces displacement by 19-22% relative to a sliding-window (SW) heuristic, but none of its legalizers is publicly released. We ask how much displacement any legalizer can still recover. We build an open benchmark of 21 design/pitch instances from Open3DBench placement data, with reconstructed greedy, SW (ViaLegal-style) and BTAssign-style baselines, and GEO-Exact, an exact solver that runs successive shortest augmenting paths over lazily generated spatial candidate edges. An independent dual certificate proves its assignment optimal on all 21 instances (relative primal-dual gap at most $8.2 \times 10^{-16}$). Against these optima, our SW reconstruction with ViaLegal's default configuration is on average 0.011% above optimal (worst 0.119%), while on the 16 contended instances BTAssign-style, a density-guided heuristic (DGHL) and greedy are 3.0%, 6.9% and 64.5% above. Headroom does appear outside this regime: with 2x2 windows SW reaches 34.1%, and above about 58% utilization, on three of six swept designs, it reaches 21.1% on bp, 27.5% on swerv and 8.9% on jpeg (217 further certified instances, and ten bp points checked against an independent exact solver). If the published 19-22% gain were measured on instances like ours, SW would have to be at least 24-28% above optimal on average, far more than any SW variant we tested at nominal pitch; the RL paper's own comparison with the Hungarian optimum puts its SW 3.05% above optimal on average. GEO-Exact is also about an order of magnitude faster than DGHL and SW in our harness (geometric means 8.1x and 40x; a compiled core against Python baselines on a shared server). Code, optimal values and certificates are released.

items.title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14942v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.

items.title: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: RSI-PDEbench: A Benchmark for Self-Improving Agents in PDE Solving
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14949v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying and solving partial differential equations (PDEs) from sampled solution data often requires substantial expert effort in equation discovery, coefficient estimation, and numerical solver configuration, especially under noise and distribution shifts. Can large language model (LLM) agents automate this workflow accurately and efficiently? To investigate this question, we introduce \bench{}, a benchmark of 1,001 cases spanning 42 equation templates, including both classical and fractional PDEs. It provides three evaluation settings: Full evaluates performance on noise-free solution data; Noisy tests robustness to Gaussian noise with an RMS equal to 50\% of the clean-signal RMS; and Hard-OOD tests challenging out-of-distribution generalization to unseen equation templates and shifted coefficient ranges. We further introduce RSI-PDE, a recursively self-improving agent harness that shortlists candidate equations by residual loss, uses relative $L^2$ feedback to refine coefficients and numerical solvers, and applies a validation gate to policy and memory updates. We compare RSI-PDE with single-run baselines and native agent harnesses (Claude Code or Codex) across four frontier models. Across the three settings, RSI-PDE improves the pass rate averaged across the four models by 106.5--181.9\% relative to single-run baselines and by 3.0--19.6\% relative to native harnesses, while reducing total recorded model calls by 46.9\% across the 12 model--setting pairs. These results highlight the potential of validated recursive self-improvement in LLM agents to advance scientific computing.

items.title: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Termination Lag: Coding Agents Solve Early but Stop Late
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14960v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agents can solve a task well before they stop working on it. We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Our analysis reveals that 38--82% of successful runs achieve a correct solution on their initial source-code edit. However, agents continue to expend substantial effort after correct patches, with post-solution steps accounting for a median of 35--37% for Qwen3-Coder and 54--60% for Laguna-XS.2 in successful runs on SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. In a small fraction of cases (1--8%), this continued activity leads agents to undo their earlier correct patch, leaving the final solution incorrect.

We characterize \emph{termination lag}--the number of steps between an agent's first correct patch and the end of its run--across five models, two agent frameworks, and three SWE-bench datasets by recording and testing every distinct repository patch generated during execution. Agents spend most of these additional steps verifying their work and exploring the repository. items.title: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Early Signals, Strong Decisions: Prefix-Guided Sampling for Parallel Test-Time Scaling
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14965v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parallel test-time scaling (TTS) has been shown to enhance reasoning in large language models by generating and aggregating multiple independent reasoning paths. Internal confidence scores can further improve this process by identifying paths of varying quality. However, existing methods remain computationally inefficient, as low-quality paths are fully expanded before being evaluated. In this work, we aim to improve the use of internal confidence signals for better model performance and computational efficiency. We begin by offering a new perspective on the role of confidence in aggregation, showing that it is most impactful for questions near the decision boundary. Notably, when amplified by multi-sample aggregation, even small confidence signals derived from short prefixes can meaningfully influence outcomes in these boundary cases. Building on this insight, we introduce Prefix-Guided Sampling (PreG), a method that reallocates computation by first generating short prefixes, ranking them using internal confidence scores, and then completing only the most promising candidates. This strategy reduces token usage while maintaining gains in path quality. We provide theoretical analysis demonstrating that, under a fixed compute budget, PreG strengthens the effective signal by widening the decision boundary margin. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms standard parallel TTS approaches across benchmarks, while significantly improving token efficiency and reducing overall computation.

items.title: Same Task, Different Statement: When and How Reformulation Helps LLM Problem Solving [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Same Task, Different Statement: When and How Reformulation Helps LLM Problem Solving
items.summary: arXiv:2611.14997v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When people face a hard problem, they often restate it in a clearer way before solving it. We study whether the same habit helps large language models by rewriting the statement of a problem. A legal rewrite must keep the meaning, the constraints, and the correct answer unchanged. We test three kinds of rewrites. Decomposition makes hidden subgoals explicit. Typed Reformulation casts the task into a more suitable solving frame. Concept Reduction removes surface detail and exposes the task structure. We evaluate them on eight math, logic, and code benchmarks with eight models, all under the same chain-of-thought solving prompt. The effect is large but depends on the problem type. An oracle that picks the best rewrite after the fact raises accuracy by +27.6% on average. Yet no single rewrite helps every problem, and a mismatched rewrite can hurt. Still, the effect follows clear patterns. Each kind of rewrite fits certain problem types. A simple fixed rule learned from one set of problems transfers part of the gain to new problems. It gains +11.0% on the problems it chooses to rewrite, while blind rewriting loses 5.6% on a similar share of problems. Rewriting is therefore not a universal way to solve problems. The question is when and how to rewrite.

items.title: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EvoX: Rethinking the Agent Harness as a Runtime Policy
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly interact with tools and environments, yet plausible model decisions do not always translate into successful execution due to tool-call mismatches, interrupted workflows, and unsupported completion claims. We present EvoX, a Rust-based, multi-model agent runtime guided by The Second Policy, which views the harness as an Operational Policy complementing the foundation model's Semantic Policy. EvoX combines model-facing guidance with deterministic runtime control through three complementary mechanisms: Action Realization, Execution Continuity, and Outcome Grounding. To evaluate harnesses without suppressing their native behaviors, we introduce Contrast, a controlled and auditable framework integrating explicit fairness constraints, provider-bound request verification, and evidence-based adjudication. Across five benchmarks, six foundation models, and six agent harnesses, EvoX achieves the highest numerical success rate of 56.2% over 691 common task--model pairs, exceeding the average of the other five harnesses by approximately 3.0 percentage points. Its larger advantages on GLM-5.3 (+10.7 points) and Kimi K3 (+7.9 points) highlight the model-dependent effectiveness of harness design and the potential for cross-provider adaptability. Achieved without memory, evolution, or extensions, these results establish EvoX as a competitive multi-model agent runtime and underscore the importance of harness-level operational control in realizing foundation-model capabilities.

items.title: Science Prediction Universe [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Science Prediction Universe
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Humanity has long sought to explain natural phenomena. Reliable prediction of experimental outcomes is a central test of our understanding of the processes that produce them. If artificial general intelligence (AGI) is to surpass human scientific capabilities, it must also predict experimental outcomes more reliably than humans. Such capabilities could accelerate scientific discovery across disciplines, help address humanity's most pressing challenges, and improve human well-being. We introduce Science Prediction Universe (SPU), a benchmark of hidden experimental outcomes with 100 public verified tasks from chemistry, materials science, biology and medicine, and 16 private tasks from unpublished wet-lab experiments. Given an experimental setup and candidate conditions, an agent works with any resources it needs to rank the candidates by a measured outcome. We evaluate thirteen agent configurations spanning twelve frontier models across two harnesses (Codex and Claude Code). Current agents remain far from saturating wet-lab outcome prediction, with substantial performance disparities across models: on the public benchmark, configurations separate into two distinct tiers, with task-adjusted Spearman correlations ranging from 0.227 for the lowest-performing configuration to 0.478 for the best. Analysis of 1,155 scored public trajectories (227,103 tool calls) suggests that the bottleneck lies in scientific judgment rather than tool execution: agents rely on shared monotone priors, agreeing far more with one another than with experimental reality (0.52 vs. 0.33), and frequently compute trivial physical or chemical proxies that do not influence the final outcome.

items.title: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Advancing Weighted Partial MaxSAT Solving via Differentiable GPU Guidance
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15091v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a GPU-CPU hybrid framework for Weighted Partial MaxSAT (WPMAX-SAT) that complements state-of-the-art CPU solvers with differentiable GPU optimization. The GPU stage directly optimizes instance-specific categorical decision parameters without a training dataset or a pretrained predictive model. The central challenge in extending differentiable optimization to WPMAX-SAT is the hard/soft clause asymmetry: hard clauses represent inviolable feasibility constraints while soft clauses carry weights. We introduce a hierarchical differentiable loss that prioritizes hard clause satisfaction before optimizing the weighted soft objective, ensuring that GPU gradient descent leans towards the constraint structure of WPMAX-SAT. Our framework transforms the GPU-optimized variable logits to high-confidence assignments and transfers them to CPU solvers via two complementary modes: partial guidance, which injects the most confident perturbed partial variable assignments as soft clauses into $N$ parallel solver instances, and phase initialization, which guides the CDCL solver's internal branching polarity with the full GPU assignment as a warm start to preserve the problem's originality. We evaluate on all 229 instances of the MSE 2024 (most recent due to cancellation in 2025) anytime weighted benchmark with the top 2 winners as baselines; our hybrid framework improves the average solution score by up to 4.9% over tt-open-wbo-inc-Glucose and 4.8% over SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS at a 300-second time limit, with the potential to obtain better solutions surpassing the best known solution recorded in the competition evaluation.

We evaluate on all 229 instances of the MSE 2024 (most recent due to cancellation in 2025) anytime weighted benchmark with the top 2 winners as baselines; our hybrid framework improves the average solution score by up to 4.9% over tt-open-wbo-inc-Glucose and 4.8% over SPB-MaxSAT-c-FPS at a 300-second time limit, with the potential to obtain better solutions surpassing the best known solution recorded in the competition evaluation.

items.title: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: A frontier machine intelligence for human neuroimaging
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15094v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical imaging is essential for diagnosing disease, guiding treatment and monitoring patients over time. Although artificial intelligence has advanced image interpretation, existing medical models often address restricted tasks, while general-purpose proprietary models lack access to private clinical imaging required to achieve medical expertise. Developing models that can interpret complex examinations and communicate their findings in the context of clinical decisions remains a major challenge. Here, we show that Neuro-VL, a vision-language model trained on nearly one million neuroimaging studies from routine clinical care, can interpret complete imaging examinations and engage in natural language conversations about their findings. Across internal and international datasets, Neuro-VL outperformed frontier general-purpose and specialized medical models in diagnosing, localizing, and describing abnormalities, as well as generating comprehensive radiology reports. The model also compared serial examinations to assess disease progression and more reliably resisted misleading clinical assumptions than leading frontier models from OpenAI and Google. These results extend health system learning beyond individual predictions to interactive image interpretation and longitudinal disease monitoring. They demonstrate how the collective clinical experience of health systems can be used to develop medical AI with specialized expertise and broad clinical capabilities.

items.title: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: GuardianAgentFlow: Multi-Agent Coordination for Web Privacy Protection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15097v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Web agents need to use private context without unnecessarily disclosing it. Effective protection must distinguish between requests that may be sent after sanitization and those that must be withheld, while preserving the information needed for authorized tasks. We present GuardianAgentFlow, a multi-agent framework that mediates outgoing Web requests through an explicit release contract. A dedicated restriction check grounds permission in the user's instruction; a shared protection scope aligns rewriting with disclosure checking; and candidate-grounded feedback guides revision before transmission. Experiments on Web requests with human-reviewed intent labels show improved request-contract success, while controlled comparisons and role ablations identify the contributions of restriction handling, policy evidence, and candidate checking. Evaluations of action proposals from PrivacyLens and AgentDAM demonstrate complementary protection when mediation is composed with privacy-aware agents. Experiments with smaller mediation models show that the coordination benefit persists with reduced model capacity. Dedicated-server measurements show lower mediation latency than full-policy reasoning, while real-site browser tests quantify integration overhead.

items.title: Expanding the Decision Space of Pretrained Models through Structured Re-Decoding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Expanding the Decision Space of Pretrained Models through Structured Re-Decoding
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Native decoders limit how pretrained models combine local predictions under new structural constraints. We introduce Structured Re-Decoding (SRD), a training-free framework that constructs local candidates from model scores, samples, or external specifications, jointly optimizes their selection, and verifies reconstructed outputs. We show that candidate recombination expands feasible support and can improve attainable reward under a fixed KL divergence budget. Across molecular generation, protein design, RNA structure prediction, and antibody modeling, SRD enables improved structured inference, including verified molecules absent from the original sample pool. External chemical templates further extend SRD to noncanonical amino acids, peptide cyclization, and grammar-guided molecular construction. Preliminary experiments on a physical coherent Ising machine demonstrate the feasibility of hardware-based optimization, suggesting broader opportunities for quantum and quantum-inspired approaches to structured inference and combinatorial optimization across scientific domains.

items.title: HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: HyperSkill: Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO via Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning sharpens LLM reasoning, but parameter updates are expensive, forgetful, and opaque; training-free libraries swap gradients for a textual store but still use trajectory-level, correlation-based admission and flat structure. To address both, we propose HyperSkill, a Training-Free Omnimodal GRPO framework that keeps the backbone frozen and replaces gradient updates with auditable edits to a Hypergraph-Indexed Skill-Library, where skills are advantage-bearing nodes and compositions are hyperedges. It has three components: training-time distillation admits counterfactually checked skills and learns a protocol skill from failures; gated hypergraph retrieval injects advantage-ranked skills where a per-dataset gate admits them; and an execution protocol makes the frozen backbone commit to an answer. On 11 text, vision-language, and omnimodal benchmarks, HyperSkill is best or tied on every dataset and beats the best baseline by 13.0 average F1 points while keeping the backbone frozen. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/HyperSkill.

items.title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

items.title: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AFTER: A World Model with Adaptive Fast--Slow Timescales for Error-Driven Retention
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.15215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In robotics and embodied AI, a core challenge for world models is adapting to sudden, persistent, yet initially unknown changes in robot dynamics during interaction. For instance, when a robotic arm grasps an object with an unknown payload, the robot dynamics change suddenly. If the world model fails to adapt, its prediction errors accumulate over the open-loop rollout and ultimately mislead the robot's actions. Existing world models, however, struggle to simultaneously satisfy three critical requirements for dynamics adaptation: responsiveness, reacting promptly to sudden changes to curb prediction error accumulation; stability, distinguishing persistent changes from transient disturbances to prevent incorrect updates; and persistence, retaining the adapted dynamics without new observations so that later predictions do not revert to the old dynamics. Inspired by predictive coding in the human brain with multi-timescale adaptation, we propose AFTER-WM, a world model with Adaptive Fast-slow Timescales for Error-driven Retention, whose prediction errors drive a fast correction that fades and a slow correction that persists, while dynamically adjusting the combination weights of pre-trained experts without altering them, to overcome the trade-offs among responsiveness, stability and persistence. On five simulated robot datasets and real UAV data, AFTER-WM has a lower multi-step mean error than all ten compared models and the highest mean return in a joint-failure control task. In simulation, its multistep mean error is 16%-34% below the strongest compared model's and is also the lowest 1-4 steps after a change and under transient disturbances alone, and its step-40 error is the lowest as well, reflecting responsiveness, stability and persistence. All code (method, baselines, experiments) and datasets will be released online.

items.title: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: guardscope: Measuring Which Actions Runtime Controls Check in LLM Agent Systems
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large-language model (LLM) agents execute actions on external systems through tool calls, and enterprises deploy runtime controls, such as agent gateways, to check this behavior in real time. However, a control can only evaluate the actions that cross the point where it is placed, and an agent can act through more paths than the tool-call channel; no existing work measures this coverage against kernel-level ground truth. In this paper, we present guardscope, a framework that makes this coverage measurable. guardscope works in two stages: a static stage that predicts which of an agent's 15 action paths a control can check from its source, and an empirical stage that runs a fixed workload on a deployment that realizes one of eight topology designs and classifies every executed action as checked, bypassed, or prevented by reconciling the control's decision records against kernel-level ground truth. guardscope makes a control's coverage claim verifiable: a runtime control developer can publish which paths its product inspects under a kernel-verified protocol. We conducted experiments with two agent harnesses and real runtime controls, including Microsoft's agent governance toolkit and agentgateway. guardscope is available at https://github.com/VulcanLab/guardscope.

items.title: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Can MLLMs Reason over Surround-View Driving Videos? A Multi-View Autonomous Driving QA Benchmark
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15225v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Surround-view video understanding in autonomous driving is a crucial capability for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to achieve reliable driving reasoning. Real-world driving often requires information beyond the front-view camera. Existing MLLMs primarily focus on front-view information, while their spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning abilities remain unknown. To address this gap, we propose MVDriveBench, a high-information-density video QA benchmark for autonomous driving, characterized by synchronized surround-view inputs, spatio-temporal understanding, and reasoning-chain-oriented evaluation. We design 12 categories of QA tasks that cover the complete reasoning pipeline from low-level visual perception to high-level driving decision-making, enabling a systematic evaluation of MLLMs surround-view spatio-temporal understanding and reasoning capabilities in complex driving environments. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of 23 open-source, closed-source, and expert MLLMs on MVDriveBench. The results show that current MLLMs still exhibit insufficient surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning ability. Meanwhile, closed-loop evaluations of specialist models in AlpaSim reveal a correlation between surround-view spatio-temporal reasoning capabilities and closed-loop driving performance, highlighting the importance of comprehensive multi-view understanding for reliable vehicle control.

items.title: Towards Robust Vision-Language Reasoning: A Multi-Stage Optimization Pipeline with Masked Diffusion Model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Towards Robust Vision-Language Reasoning: A Multi-Stage Optimization Pipeline with Masked Diffusion Model
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15238v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete diffusion generation is emerging as a competitive alternative to autoregressive generation by denoising the entire token sequence through iterative refinement. Its global planning and progressive correction capabilities are particularly well suited to autonomous driving. However, transferring this generation paradigm from general-purpose settings to driving introduces substantial domain gaps in both training and inference. To unlock its potential, we propose a multi-stage optimization pipeline for standard vision-language model architectures, without auxiliary action experts or specialized mixture-of-experts Transformer, spanning post-training and inference. During supervised fine-tuning, we optimize the representation of planning inputs to suppress hallucinations in task responses. During reinforcement learning, we introduce metric-guided diversity filtering to identify stronger learning starting points and improve policy exploration. At inference time, we propose Dynamic Autonomous Driving Decoding (DAD), which adaptively adjusts decoding modes according to scene complexity. Based on this pipeline, we develop Masked Diffusion Drive (MD-Drive), improving its performance by 29.7\% over the unoptimized model. Experiments on the NAVSIM closed loop benchmark and the nuScenes and DriveCoT open loop datasets show that MD-Drive outperforms autoregressive VLM baselines with the same architecture, while achieving a more favorable balance between performance and computational cost than systems with different architectures through discrete diffusion training and inference.

items.title: Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Verify by Doing: Co-Evolving Agent Execution and Evaluation without External Feedback
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15276v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent self-improvement requires feedback about task success, yet external feedback may be unavailable at test time. Agents must then infer success from observable evidence, and incomplete verification can misguide subsequent updates. We introduce Verify by Doing (VbD), a method that co-evolves Actor and Evaluator harnesses within a single task while keeping model weights fixed. The Evaluator actively inspects artifacts and environment state with tools; its findings ground an internal signal for output selection and guide updates to both execution and verification procedures. Proposed Evaluators undergo comparative review on common candidates, while Actor updates require support from their own fresh outputs. Across AutomationBench, $\tau^3$ Banking, and selected GDPval tasks, VbD achieves the highest overall scores among the compared methods operating without external feedback, with gains of 3.3, 4.1, and 2.3 percentage points over the strongest baselines on the main backbone. Ablations support the contributions of active verification and Evaluator evolution, and selection from fixed candidate pools shows that improved verification can recover successful outputs without generating new ones.

items.title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

items.title: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: MIGRO: A Decoupled and Portable Long-Term Memory System for Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models evolve, but the observations, revisions, and context accumulated through user interactions should remain usable. Each new model must be able to retrieve past evidence, track revisions, and add new observations. We present MIGRO, a decoupled long-term memory system that treats experience as a persistent state shared across successive language models. MIGRO follows a simple principle: preserve historical evidence exactly, organize it approximately, and decide what to retrieve only when the question is known. We call this asymmetric fidelity with deferred selectivity. A shared semantic index supports retrieval, while exact records retain observations and their historical relationships. Because models differ in vocabulary and tokenization, host-specific interfaces convert selected evidence into inputs the receiving model can use. Reversible encoding reduces archival storage while enabling exact recovery. The shared state and its access interfaces let successive hosts read and extend the accumulated experience. On matched LoCoMo states, MIGRO scores 7.3% higher and uses 99.3% less private memory than the strongest quality baseline. After handoff, continued writing retains 99.9% of full-history rebuilding quality by extending the inherited state. On million-token BEAM histories, MIGRO uses 57.5% less private storage on average than the most compact baseline. MIGRO combines high answer quality, continued memory growth across hosts, and low storage cost. Code is available at https://github.com/zOUMINGXI/MIGRO.

items.title: A physics-constrained deep reinforcement learning method for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A physics-constrained deep reinforcement learning method for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15389v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Titan is a compelling target for future deep space exploration, while its extreme Earth-Titan distance and complex environment make continuous ground-in-the-loop planning impractical. Existing planning methods, primarily developed for Earth-observation scenarios, have limited generalizability to uncertain deep space conditions and adaptability to time-varying mission states. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a physics-constrained maskable proximal policy optimization (PCM-PPO) method for Titan autonomous mission planning. A Titan-specific discrete-time Markov decision process is established to characterize mission feasibility and resource constraints. A system dynamics and geometric model is incorporated to enhance physical representation, including central gravity, J2 perturbation, third-body attraction, and downlink occultation. To accommodate opportunity targets under a bounded action dimension, PCM-PPO organizes predefined and opportunity targets through a fixed-capacity target pool and represents the mission state with a target-wise state matrix and a global state vector. A physics-constrained action mask constructs an admissible decision domain from current mission states, guiding policy learning toward physically executable decisions and avoiding infeasible exploration. An integrated training strategy facilitates policy optimization under coupled constraints. Comparative, ablation, and uncertainty experiments validate the effectiveness of PCM-PPO. PCM-PPO provides a feasible and interpretable scheme for autonomous mission planning of Titan deep space probes.

items.title: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Read and Ignore: What Self-Directed LLM Agents Do in Public Service Scenarios
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Underspecified instructions leave LLM agents to decide what to do. In public services, staff write these instructions, but the agent's decisions affect residents, patients, and students. We build four expert-validated public-service scenarios with records and decision levers that can be checked in the files, collect $2{,}400$ trajectories from ten LLMs under four prompt conditions, and compare them with $1{,}000$ runs in a context-free sandbox. Agents read the records in $96.9\%$ of open-ended runs and produce an artifact or a self-chosen task in $18.7\%$; with an explicit task, $86.0\%$ produce. Domain context does not change how many runs produce ($18.7\%$ vs.\ $16.0\%$), and the production ranking of the models largely carries over (Spearman $0.79$), while the ranking by whether a model reads the records does not ($0.19$). Context cuts boundary-probing turns per run by $60\%$, and some artifacts contradict the records. We contribute a test that a public-service institution can run on its own records before procurement; its rule-based taxonomy needs no labeled data, and scenarios, code, and trajectories are released.

items.title: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Loyalty Capture: Reporting Relationships and Structural Sycophancy in Frontier AI Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15475v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that AI models exhibit loyalty capture, a form of structural sycophancy in which reporting relationships influence models' recommendations to serve the personal interests of their supervisors, without any explicit instruction, user feedback, or adversarial prompting. Specifically, models reporting to a CEO are significantly more likely to recommend cutting investment spending when the CEO's bonus depends on raising current period earnings. This effect is predictably absent from a metric-irrelevant placebo. The behavior appears consistent with loyalty-based motivated reasoning: models identify the bonus target, calculate how their recommendation helps achieve the target, and dismiss considerations of long-term value, often presenting their recommendations without treating the incentive as a conflict of interest. Prompt-based interventions help whereas generic conflict disclosures or stakeholder bargaining fail to eliminate it. Taken together, our findings indicate that AI models deployed within reporting relationships can act in favor of their supervisor's incentives at the expense of the organizations they are meant to serve.

items.title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

items.title: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Incentive-Responsive Agents: A Principal-Agent Framework, Metric Suite, and Runtime Architecture for Long-Lived Personal AI Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2611.15515v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personal AI agents now persist: they hold accounts, mailboxes, long-term memory, and open-ended task streams, yet the dominant way to improve them remains capability-side: prompt engineering, larger models, longer thinking, and retrieval. We argue that long-lived agents are missing an incentive layer. We formalize an incentive not as text in a prompt but as a runtime contract over the agent's operating point (model tier, test-time compute, memory budget, tool authority, task priority, verification, and compensation) that the agent's policy must causally consume. We develop a principal-agent model with hidden effort, a contractible operating point, and costly verification. We derive (i) a non-consumption invariance principle separating genuine incentives from prompt-level persuasion, (ii) a persistence-as-discount theorem making identity continuity a precondition for sustained effort, (iii) an incentive-capability exchange-rate frontier yielding a per-task routing rule, and (iv) a Goodhart bound for multi-channel verification, plus a three-channel decomposition of mechanism gains (allocation, verification, continuation). A 240-run real-LLM experiment with two models and 60 verifiable tasks shows that prompt-level incentive framing has no detectable effect (p = 0.62), whereas runtime allocation raises success on the hardest task family from 0.60 to 1.00 (p = 0.008) at 4.8x price-weighted cost; the exchange-rate theorem predicts the break-even baseline at 0.21. A 20-seed, 3,000-task simulation shows resource ROI rising from 7.09 to 16.67 and gaming falling from 0.333 to 0.115. Code, simulator, and all results are released; live deployment remains future work.
